meaning: A friendly opening line for an email.
useWhen: Starting an email to someone you know a little.
example: Hi Priya, hope you're doing well. Sharing the plan for next week.
careful: Use it once, at the start. Skip it in quick replies on a busy thread.

wrong.label: ✗ Not as a closing line
wrong.text: Please send the report today. Hope you're doing well.

similar: Hope your week is going well.

meaning: Ravi still gets this email, but later replies won't include him.
useWhen: Someone introduced you, and now you two talk directly.
example: Thanks for the intro, Ravi! Moving Ravi to BCC. Hi Meera, great to meet you.
careful: Say it at the top, so Ravi knows why the replies stop.

wrong.label: ✗ He still gets this email
wrong.text: Moving Ravi to BCC, so he won't see this message.

similar: Moving you to BCC to spare your inbox.
Taking you off the thread now.

meaning: The file you need is attached to this email.
useWhen: You send a file with the email.
example: Please find attached the signed contract.
careful: Name the file. In casual emails, "I've attached it" sounds friendlier.

wrong.label: ✗ Only when a file is attached
wrong.text: Please find attached my thoughts in the email below.

similar: Here's the file you asked for.

meaning: I'm adding the finance team to this email.
useWhen: Others need to see the thread or help with it.
example: Looping in the finance team, as they handle refunds.
careful: Say why you're adding them, so they know what to do.

wrong.label: ✗ It means adding, not removing
wrong.text: Looping in the finance team, so they stop getting these emails.

meaning: As I already said in my earlier email.
useWhen: Someone asks again about something you already answered.
example: Per my last email, the deadline is 12 May.
careful: It often reads as irritated. Softer: "As I mentioned earlier."

wrong.label: ✗ Only when you're repeating a point
wrong.text: Per my last email, happy birthday!

similar: As I said in my email,

meaning: Thank you for answering so fast.
useWhen: Someone replied sooner than you expected.
example: Thanks for your quick reply. That solves it.
careful: Only if it really was quick. After a week, it sounds sarcastic.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a slow reply
wrong.text: Thanks for your quick reply after three weeks.

similar: Thanks for getting back so fast.

meaning: Here is what we agreed when we spoke.
useWhen: Writing after a call to put the points in writing.
example: As discussed on the call, we'll launch on Monday.
careful: List only what you both agreed. Don't slip in new points.

wrong.label: ✗ Only if there was a call
wrong.text: As discussed on the call, here's my first message to you.

similar: As we agreed on the call,

topic: Let me know if you have any questions.
phrase: Let me know if you have any questions.
meaning: Ask me if anything is unclear.
useWhen: Ending an email that explains something.
example: The steps are below. Let me know if you have any questions.
careful: Mean it, and reply quickly when they do ask.

wrong.label: ✗ Not after a simple thank-you
wrong.text: Thanks for lunch! Let me know if you have any questions.

topic: Please feel free to reach out.
phrase: Please feel free to reach out.
meaning: You are welcome to contact me anytime.
useWhen: Offering help to a client or a new contact.
example: If you need anything for the event, please feel free to reach out.
careful: Add how to reach you, by email or phone. Otherwise it feels empty.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for something they must do
wrong.text: Please feel free to reach out and pay the bill today.

similar: Don't hesitate to get in touch.

meaning: To finish this topic and tell everyone the final result.
useWhen: Giving the last update on something that was open.
example: To close the loop, the client approved the design today.
careful: Use it when the matter is truly finished.

wrong.label: ✗ Not to start a new topic
wrong.text: To close the loop, I want to propose a new project.

topic: Looking forward to hearing from you.
phrase: Looking forward to hearing from you.
meaning: I hope you reply soon.
useWhen: Ending an email that needs an answer.
example: I've shared the quote. Looking forward to hearing from you.
careful: Fine for clients. With teammates, "Let me know" is lighter.

wrong.label: ✗ Not after they said no
wrong.text: Thanks for telling me you're not interested. Looking forward to hearing from you.

similar: I look forward to your reply.
Hope to hear from you soon.

topic: I wanted to check in on the proposal.
phrase: I wanted to check in on the proposal.
meaning: I'm politely asking for an update on the proposal.
useWhen: You sent something and haven't heard back.
example: Hi Sameer, I wanted to check in on the proposal we sent last week.
careful: Add one clear question, like "Any decision yet?"

wrong.label: ✗ Not a hotel check-in
wrong.text: I wanted to check in on the proposal at 2 p.m. with my bags.

similar: Just following up on the proposal.

meaning: I'm sorry I took long to answer.
useWhen: You reply days after their email.
example: Sorry for the late reply. Here are the numbers you asked for.
careful: Say it once, then give the answer. No long excuses.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a fast reply
wrong.text: (sent five minutes later) Sorry for the late reply.

similar: Sorry it took me a while.

topic: Just a quick note to say thanks.
phrase: Just a quick note to say thanks.
meaning: A short email only to thank someone.
useWhen: Someone helped and you want to thank them in writing.
example: Just a quick note to say thanks for covering the client call.
careful: Keep it short, and name what they did.

wrong.label: ✗ Not to sneak in a big request
wrong.text: Just a quick note to say thanks. Also, here are ten tasks for you.

similar: Thanks so much for your help.
Wanted to say a big thank you.

meaning: Here is a short summary of what we said.
useWhen: Ending a long thread or writing call notes.
example: Just to recap: Neha sends the draft, and we review on Friday.
careful: Keep the recap shorter than the talk. Bullet points help.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for brand-new information
wrong.text: Just to recap, here is a new plan nobody has seen.

meaning: Thank you now for help you will give.
useWhen: Asking for a small favour.
example: Could you share the slides by noon? Thanks in advance.
careful: It can sound like they have no choice. For big asks, thank them afterwards.

wrong.label: ✗ Not after they've helped
wrong.text: You fixed it yesterday. Thanks in advance!

similar: Thanks for your help with this.

meaning: I hope my answer is useful.
useWhen: Ending an email where you answered a question.
example: The form is on page 3. Hope this helps.
careful: Use it after giving help, not after giving an order.

wrong.label: ✗ Not after bad news
wrong.text: Your leave request is rejected. Hope this helps.

similar: Let me know if you need more.

meaning: The details are further down in this email.
useWhen: Your answer or the old thread sits under your short note.
example: Please see below for the meeting notes.
careful: Make sure there really is something below.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for an attached file
wrong.text: Please see below the PDF I attached.

topic: Could you shed some light on this?
phrase: Could you shed some light on this?
meaning: Could you explain this to me?
useWhen: Something is unclear and they know more.
example: The bill has a new charge. Could you shed some light on this?
careful: Say what exactly is unclear, so they can answer fast.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about real lights
wrong.text: The room is too dark. Could you shed some light on this?

similar: Could you help me understand this?

meaning: Please tell me what I should do.
useWhen: You need a decision from someone senior or an expert.
example: The vendor wants a 10% price rise. Please advise.
careful: Alone, it can feel cold. Add the options: "Should we accept or push back?"

wrong.label: ✗ Not for sharing news
wrong.text: I got married last week. Please advise.

similar: How would you like me to proceed?

meaning: The file is with this email.
useWhen: You send a document in a normal email.
example: I've attached the file. The totals are on the second sheet.
careful: Check the file is really attached before you hit send.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for paper on a desk
wrong.text: I've attached the file to your desk with tape.

meaning: I'll tell you when there is news.
useWhen: Something is still in progress.
example: The courier hasn't confirmed yet. I'll keep you posted.
careful: Then actually send the update, even if it's "no news yet".

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a finished task
wrong.text: The job is done and closed. I'll keep you posted.

meaning: Please tell me yes or no, so I know for sure.
useWhen: You need a clear answer before you act.
example: We have you down for Tuesday at 4. Could you please confirm?
careful: Say what to confirm: the date, the price or the name.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for an open question
wrong.text: What did you think of the movie? Could you please confirm?

similar: Please let me know if that's right.

topic: Let me know if that works for you.
phrase: Let me know if that works for you.
meaning: Tell me if this plan suits you.
useWhen: You suggest a time or a plan.
example: How about Thursday at 11? Let me know if that works for you.
careful: Offer a second option if you can.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a fixed order
wrong.text: You must submit it today. Let me know if that works for you.

meaning: The decision or next step is yours now.
useWhen: You've given all the facts and they must decide.
example: Both quotes are attached. I'll leave it with you.
careful: It ends your part. Don't use it when you still owe them work.

wrong.label: ✗ Not when you still have work to do
wrong.text: I'll leave it with you, and I'll finish my part tomorrow.

meaning: I've read it and I'll keep it in mind.
useWhen: A short reply to an update or instruction.
example: The office is closed on Friday. — Noted, thanks.
careful: Very short, so it can feel cold. Add a line if their email was long or kind.

wrong.label: ✗ Not as an answer to a question
wrong.text: Can you join at 3? — Noted, thanks.

meaning: Thank you for pointing out this problem.
useWhen: Someone warns you about a mistake or risk.
example: Good catch on the wrong date. Thanks for flagging this.
careful: Then say what you'll do about it.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about real flags
wrong.text: Thanks for flagging this for Independence Day.

meaning: I was glad to help you.
useWhen: Replying when someone thanks you.
example: Thanks for the notes! — Happy to help.
careful: Short and kind. It closes the thread nicely.

wrong.label: ✗ Not when they helped you
wrong.text: You fixed my laptop. Happy to help!

topic: Happy to jump on a call.
phrase: Happy to jump on a call.
meaning: I'm willing to talk on the phone or a video call.
useWhen: The email thread is getting long or confusing.
example: This is tricky by email. Happy to jump on a call if that's easier.
careful: Suggest a time, or ask for theirs.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for meeting in person
wrong.text: Happy to jump on a call at your office desk tomorrow.

similar: Shall we discuss on a call?

meaning: Adding to the email I sent before.
useWhen: You send extra details after your own earlier email.
example: Further to my email this morning, here is the updated price list.
careful: Quite formal. With teammates, "Adding to my last email" is fine.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a first email
wrong.text: Further to my email, let me introduce myself.

similar: Following up on my earlier email,

meaning: Thank you for contacting me.
useWhen: Replying to someone who wrote to you first.
example: Thanks for reaching out. Yes, we deliver to Pune.
careful: Use it when they started the conversation, not you.

wrong.label: ✗ Not when you wrote first
wrong.text: Hi, I'm Karan from sales. Thanks for reaching out.

topic: I'm reaching out about the order.
phrase: I'm reaching out about the order.
meaning: I'm writing to you about the order.
useWhen: Starting a first email, so they know the topic.
example: Hi team, I'm reaching out about the order placed on 3 June.
careful: Give the order number in the same line.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for reaching with your hand
wrong.text: The box is up high, so I'm reaching out about the order.

similar: I have a question about the order.

topic: I'll get back to you by Friday.
phrase: I'll get back to you by Friday.
meaning: I'll reply with an answer no later than Friday.
useWhen: You need time but want to give a clear date.
example: Let me check with the team. I'll get back to you by Friday.
careful: Keep the date. If you can't, write before Friday to say so.

wrong.label: ✗ "By Friday" means no later than Friday
wrong.text: I'll get back to you by Friday, sometime next month.

similar: You'll hear from me by Friday.
I'll reply by the end of the week.

meaning: Please handle this before your other work.
useWhen: Something truly can't wait.
example: The site is down for customers. Please treat this as urgent.
careful: Use it rarely, and say why. If you overuse it, people ignore it.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for small things
wrong.text: Please treat this as urgent: where are the spare pens?

meaning: I'm adding Arjun so he can see this, not so he acts on it.
useWhen: A senior or teammate should know what's happening.
example: Copying Arjun for visibility, since he owns the budget.
careful: Copying a boss can feel like a threat. Use it to inform, not to complain.

wrong.label: ✗ Not when you need him to act
wrong.text: Copying Arjun for visibility. Arjun, please fix this today.

meaning: I'm including Neha in this email chain.
useWhen: Someone new needs to join the conversation.
example: Adding Neha to the thread. She handles bookings.
careful: Tell her what she needs to read or do.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about sewing
wrong.text: Adding Neha to the thread, so she can fix my button.

meaning: My manager can see this email too.
useWhen: Your manager should know, or may need to decide.
example: I've copied my manager, as this needs her approval.
careful: Give a reason, or it can sound like you're complaining to the boss.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about copying someone's work
wrong.text: I've copied my manager's answers into my test.

meaning: My earlier email was a mistake. Don't act on it.
useWhen: You sent something wrong or too early.
example: Please ignore my last email. The correct date is the 14th.
careful: Give the correct information in the same email.

wrong.label: ✗ Not if the email still stands
wrong.text: Please ignore my last email. I meant every word of it.

similar: Sorry, my last email was wrong.

meaning: Please tell me you got this email or file.
useWhen: Sending something important, like a contract or payment.
example: The signed contract is attached. Please confirm receipt.
careful: Use it only for important items, not every email.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about a shop bill
wrong.text: Please confirm receipt: was the bill ₹250 or ₹300?

similar: Could you confirm you got this?
Please let me know it arrived.

meaning: I can explain in more detail if you want.
useWhen: You kept the email short on purpose.
example: That's the short version. Happy to elaborate if needed.
careful: It's an offer, so keep the email itself short.

wrong.label: ✗ Not after a very long email
wrong.text: Here are twelve pages on the plan. Happy to elaborate if needed.

similar: I can explain more if that helps.

meaning: I didn't notice your email earlier.
useWhen: You find an email you overlooked.
example: Sorry, I missed this. Yes, Monday works.
careful: Give the answer right after it. Don't over-apologise.

wrong.label: ✗ Not on its own — add the answer
wrong.text: Can you send the report? — Sorry, I missed this.

meaning: Thank you for accepting this problem calmly.
useWhen: You give bad news, like a delay or a change.
example: The shop is closed on Monday. Thanks for your understanding.
careful: Some people find it pushy. "Thanks for your patience" can feel softer.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about knowing a subject
wrong.text: Thanks for your understanding of algebra.

meaning: A friendly goodbye before the weekend.
useWhen: Ending an email on Friday afternoon.
example: The draft is attached. Have a great weekend.
careful: Only on a Friday, or late on Thursday.

wrong.label: ✗ Not at the start of the week
wrong.text: Happy Monday! Have a great weekend.

meaning: I'd like your opinion on this.
useWhen: Asking a colleague to share ideas.
example: Here's the first draft. I'd appreciate your input on the title.
careful: Say which part, and by when.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for typing in data
wrong.text: I'd appreciate your input of 500 rows into the sheet.

topic: Let me know if I've missed anything.
phrase: Let me know if I've missed anything.
meaning: Tell me if I left something out.
useWhen: Sending a summary or list for others to check.
example: Notes from today are below. Let me know if I've missed anything.
careful: Then add what they send, and thank them.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a personal message
wrong.text: Happy birthday, Mum! Let me know if I've missed anything.

similar: Feel free to add anything I missed.

meaning: A polite way to end an email, before your name.
useWhen: Signing off a work email.
example: Thanks again for your time. Best regards, Anita
careful: Fine for almost any work email. With close teammates, "Thanks" is enough.

wrong.label: ✗ Only at the end, before your name
wrong.text: Best regards, can you send the file?

meaning: These are the key points, in short.
useWhen: A long thread or report needs a short version.
example: Here's a quick summary: we're on budget, but two weeks late.
careful: Keep it quick: three points at most.

wrong.label: ✗ Not before a long essay
wrong.text: Here's a quick summary, in twenty paragraphs.

meaning: A warm, polite email sign-off.
useWhen: Ending an email to a client or someone you don't know well.
example: Please find the quote attached. Kind regards, Karan
careful: "Regards" alone can seem cold. "Kind regards" is safer.

wrong.label: ✗ Too formal for a friend's text
wrong.text: Movie at 7? Kind regards, Karan

topic: Can we set up a quick call?
phrase: Can we set up a quick call?
meaning: Can we plan a short phone or video call?
useWhen: An issue is easier to talk through than to type.
example: Can we set up a quick call to agree on the timeline?
careful: Offer two time slots to save back-and-forth.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a long workshop
wrong.text: Can we set up a quick call? It will take all day.

similar: Could we hop on a call?
Do you have 15 minutes to talk?

meaning: Thank you for waiting patiently while we fix this.
useWhen: A delay or problem affects a customer or client.
example: Your order is now on its way. Thanks for bearing with us.
careful: It's spelled "bearing", not "baring".

wrong.label: ✗ Wrong spelling
wrong.text: Thanks for baring with us.

meaning: Thank you for telling me the latest news.
useWhen: Someone shares progress or a change.
example: Thanks for the update. Glad the shipment left on time.
careful: Add one line that shows you read it.

wrong.label: ✗ Not when you gave the update
wrong.text: Here's my progress report. Thanks for the update.

topic: I'm writing to ask about the delivery date.
phrase: I'm writing to ask about the delivery date.
meaning: The reason for my email is the delivery date.
useWhen: Opening a first email to a company or supplier.
example: I'm writing to ask about the delivery date for order 4471.
careful: Put the question in the first line, as here.

wrong.label: ✗ Not on a phone call
wrong.text: Hello, it's Priya on the phone. I'm writing to ask about the delivery date.

similar: I'd like to check the delivery date.
Could you tell me the delivery date?

topic: Please let me know your thoughts.
phrase: Please let me know your thoughts.
meaning: Please tell me what you think.
useWhen: You share a draft, a plan or an idea.
example: The new logo is attached. Please let me know your thoughts.
careful: Add a date if you need the reply soon.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a plain yes-or-no fact
wrong.text: Is the office open on Sunday? Please let me know your thoughts.

topic: I'll pass this on to the team.
phrase: I'll pass this on to the team.
meaning: I'll share this message with my team.
useWhen: Someone sends praise, feedback or a request for the team.
example: Thank you for the kind words. I'll pass this on to the team.
careful: Then actually forward it.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for something private
wrong.text: Thanks for sharing your health news. I'll pass this on to the team.

similar: I'll share this with the team.

meaning: About the email you sent me.
useWhen: Replying formally to one specific email.
example: With reference to your email of 2 March, the refund has been sent.
careful: Very formal. In most emails, "About your email" is enough.

wrong.label: ✗ Too formal for a quick chat
wrong.text: With reference to your email, lunch at 1?

meaning: I have one short question about the bill.
useWhen: A subject line or first line for one small question.
example: Quick question about the invoice: does it include tax?
careful: Keep it to one question, so it stays quick.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a long list
wrong.text: Quick question about the invoice. I have fifteen points below.

meaning: Reply to everyone on this email, not just me.
useWhen: The whole group needs to see the answers.
example: Please reply all, so the whole team sees your dates.
careful: Ask for it only when everyone truly needs the replies.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a private answer
wrong.text: Please reply all with your salary details.

meaning: I'm not working today, so my replies will be slow.
useWhen: Telling people you're away for the day.
example: I'm out of office today. I'll reply tomorrow morning.
careful: Give a backup contact for anything urgent.

wrong.label: ✗ Not when you're working as usual
wrong.text: I'm out of office today, so I'll join all my meetings.

meaning: Thank you for reminding me.
useWhen: Someone reminds you of a task or a date.
example: Thanks for the reminder. I'll send it by noon.
careful: Add when you'll do it.

wrong.label: ✗ Not when you reminded them
wrong.text: Don't forget the report! Thanks for the reminder.

meaning: Thanks for gently reminding me.
useWhen: Someone gently reminded you about something you forgot.
example: Thanks for the nudge. The form is filled in now.
careful: Informal. Fine with colleagues, less so with a strict client.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a real push
wrong.text: Thanks for the nudge. I fell down the stairs.

meaning: A soft way to remind someone about a task.
useWhen: A deadline is near and they haven't replied.
example: Gentle reminder: timesheets are due today.
careful: Don't send many. A second reminder can be clearer.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a scolding
wrong.text: Gentle reminder: you are lazy and always late.

meaning: Please tell me.
useWhen: Ending an email warmly, inviting a reply.
example: If you'd like a second copy, do let me know.
careful: "Do" adds warmth, not pressure. "Let me know" alone is lighter.

wrong.label: ✗ Not a demand
wrong.text: Do let me know in ten minutes, or else.

meaning: Thank you for waiting without complaint.
useWhen: Someone waited for your reply or a fix.
example: Thanks for your patience. The issue is now fixed.
careful: It thanks them, which lands better than "Sorry for the delay" alone.

wrong.label: ✗ Not if they haven't waited
wrong.text: Hi, this is my first email. Thanks for your patience.

meaning: I'm sorry to write to you one more time.
useWhen: You follow up a second or third time.
example: Sorry to bother you again. Any update on the visa letter?
careful: Don't over-apologise. A clear question matters more.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a first email
wrong.text: Hi, I'm new here. Sorry to bother you again.

meaning: You can disagree with me openly.
useWhen: You share an idea and want honest views.
example: This is my first plan. Feel free to push back on the dates.
careful: Mean it. If they disagree, thank them.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about pushing objects
wrong.text: Feel free to push back the heavy door.

meaning: I'm sorry if my message was unclear.
useWhen: You correct something you said badly.
example: Sorry for any confusion. The meeting is at 3, not 2.
careful: Give the clear version right after.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a big mistake
wrong.text: We lost all your data. Sorry for any confusion.

meaning: We can talk more about this if you want.
useWhen: Ending an email on an open topic.
example: That's my view on the pricing. I'm happy to discuss further.
careful: Say how: a call, a meeting or by email.

wrong.label: ✗ Not to end the talk
wrong.text: I'm happy to discuss further. Please don't reply.

meaning: Please send me the newest copy of the file.
useWhen: Several drafts exist and you need the current one.
example: Please share the latest version of the slides before 4.
careful: Name the file, so they send the right one.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for an old copy
wrong.text: Please share the latest version from last year.

similar: Could you send the newest draft?
Can I get the current file?

meaning: Please send the link one more time.
useWhen: You lost the link, or it doesn't open.
example: Sorry, I can't find the invite. Could you resend the link?
careful: Search your inbox first, then ask.

wrong.label: ✗ Not if it was never sent
wrong.text: We've never spoken before. Could you resend the link?

similar: Could you share the link again?
Can you send the link once more?

meaning: Let me tell you now what will and won't happen.
useWhen: Warning early about limits, timing or cost.
example: Just to set expectations, the first draft will be rough.
careful: Say it early, before anyone is disappointed.

wrong.label: ✗ Not after the problem
wrong.text: The launch failed. Just to set expectations, it might fail.

similar: So you know what to expect,

meaning: We have to start again from the beginning.
useWhen: A plan fails and the work is lost.
example: The client rejected the design, so we're back to square one.
careful: Use it for real restarts, not small changes.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for good progress
wrong.text: We finished early! We're back to square one.

meaning: The idea failed, so we need a new plan.
useWhen: A plan or design doesn't work.
example: The test users hated it. Back to the drawing board.
careful: It sounds positive, like "let's try again". Good after a setback.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about art class
wrong.text: I love painting, so back to the drawing board at 5.

meaning: It's very easy.
useWhen: A task is simple for you.
example: Setting up the printer? It's a piece of cake.
careful: Don't say it about someone else's hard work. It can belittle them.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for something hard
wrong.text: This exam is really tough. It's a piece of cake.

topic: Can you give me a ballpark figure?
phrase: Can you give me a ballpark figure?
meaning: Can you give me a rough number?
useWhen: You need an estimate, not an exact amount.
example: Before the full quote, can you give me a ballpark figure?
careful: Treat the answer as rough. Don't hold them to it.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for an exact number
wrong.text: Can you give me a ballpark figure, to the last rupee?

similar: Can you give me a rough estimate?

meaning: Let's do the hard or unpleasant thing now.
useWhen: Waiting won't make it easier.
example: The old system keeps crashing. Let's bite the bullet and replace it.
careful: Use it for a tough choice, not an easy one.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for something fun
wrong.text: Let's bite the bullet and go for ice cream.

meaning: Let's do something to help people relax.
useWhen: Starting a meeting with strangers or a quiet group.
example: Let's break the ice: everyone, share one hobby.
careful: Keep the ice-breaker short and easy.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about real ice
wrong.text: Let's break the ice in the freezer tray.

similar: Let's get to know each other.

topic: The ball is in your court.
phrase: The ball is in your court.
meaning: It's your turn to decide or act.
useWhen: You've done your part and are waiting for them.
example: We've sent our offer. The ball is in your court.
careful: It can sound like pressure. Add a soft line: "No rush."

wrong.label: ✗ Not when you still need to act
wrong.text: I haven't replied yet, so the ball is in your court.

meaning: Keep telling me what's happening.
useWhen: You're not doing the work but want updates.
example: You two handle the vendor. Keep me in the loop.
careful: Say how often you want updates.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about a running track
wrong.text: Keep me in the loop around the park.

similar: Let me know how it goes.

topic: Let's go for the low-hanging fruit.
phrase: Let's go for the low-hanging fruit.
meaning: Let's do the easy, quick wins first.
useWhen: Planning where to start.
example: Let's go for the low-hanging fruit: fix the typos first.
careful: Common in offices, but some find it overused.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for the hardest task
wrong.text: Let's go for the low-hanging fruit: rebuild the whole app.

similar: Let's start with the quick wins.

meaning: They keep changing the rules or targets.
useWhen: Someone keeps changing what they want.
example: First a blue logo, now red. They keep moving the goalposts.
careful: It's a complaint. Don't write it to that same client.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a fixed plan
wrong.text: They agreed the brief in May and never changed it. They keep moving the goalposts.

similar: They keep changing what they want.

meaning: It sounds simple, but it's hard to do.
useWhen: Someone suggests a fix that is hard in real life.
example: "Just finish it this week." Easier said than done.
careful: Don't stop there. Say what would make it possible.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for an easy task
wrong.text: Turn the light on? Easier said than done.

similar: That's not as easy as it sounds.
If only it were that simple.

meaning: Let's not skip steps to save time or money.
useWhen: Quality or safety matters.
example: It's a hospital app. Let's not cut corners on testing.
careful: Say which step must not be skipped.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about paper
wrong.text: Let's not cut corners off the poster.

meaning: Doing it late is better than not doing it.
useWhen: Something arrives late, but it still helps.
example: Your birthday card is a week late. Better late than never!
careful: Fine for small things. For a missed client deadline, apologise instead.

wrong.label: ✗ Not as an excuse to a client
wrong.text: We missed your launch by a month. Better late than never!

topic: We need to think outside the box.
phrase: We need to think outside the box.
meaning: We need new, creative ideas.
useWhen: The usual ideas aren't working.
example: The ads aren't working. We need to think outside the box.
careful: Very common. Give one example idea, so it doesn't sound empty.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for doing the usual thing
wrong.text: Let's do exactly what we did last year. We need to think outside the box.

meaning: Understand the hidden meaning, not just the words.
useWhen: Someone hints at something without saying it.
example: He called the plan "interesting". Read between the lines: he's not convinced.
careful: Your guess may be wrong. Ask if it matters.

wrong.label: ✗ Not about line spacing
wrong.text: Read between the lines; the text is double-spaced.

meaning: It's time to leave.
useWhen: Ending a visit or a long day.
example: It's 7 already. Time to hit the road.
careful: Casual. Fine with colleagues, not in a formal email.

wrong.label: ✗ Not when you've just arrived
wrong.text: I just got here. Time to hit the road.

topic: You'll get the hang of it.
phrase: You'll get the hang of it.
meaning: You'll learn how to do it soon.
useWhen: Encouraging someone who is new to a task.
example: The new tool feels hard at first. You'll get the hang of it.
careful: Offer help too, not just the line.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for an expert
wrong.text: You've done this for twenty years. You'll get the hang of it.

meaning: Let's start now.
useWhen: Beginning a project or a meeting.
example: Everyone's here, so let's get the ball rolling.
careful: Follow it with the first step, so people know where to begin.

wrong.label: ✗ Not at the end
wrong.text: Great meeting, everyone. Let's get the ball rolling. Bye!

meaning: It's uncertain. It could go either way.
useWhen: You're not sure something will work out.
example: The flight is delayed. It's touch and go if we make the meeting.
careful: Say the risk clearly if people need to plan.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for a sure thing
wrong.text: We finished yesterday. It's touch and go.

meaning: Let's not act too early.
useWhen: Someone wants to act before the facts are clear.
example: The results aren't final. Let's not jump the gun on the press release.
careful: Say what you're waiting for, and when.

wrong.label: ✗ Not for being late
wrong.text: We're a week behind. Let's not jump the gun.
